title: Preparation and Delivery Preparación y Entrega

blocks.en: Unit Eight · Stage 5: Prepare and Deliver
blocks.es_reference: Unidad Ocho · Etapa 5: Preparar y Predicar

blocks.en: Preparation and Delivery
blocks.es_reference: Preparación y Entrega

blocks.en: Weekly preparation rhythm, methods of delivery, voice, body, eye contact — turning the manuscript into a living sermon.
blocks.es_reference: Ritmo semanal de preparación, métodos de entrega, voz, cuerpo, contacto visual — convirtiendo el manuscrito en un sermón vivo.

blocks.en: 8.1 Collecting Ideas and Materials
blocks.es_reference: 8.1 Recogiendo Ideas y Materiales

blocks.en: Specific preparation is the preparation that you do in your weekly routine. Many preachers find weekly sermon preparation exhausting. Reader's Digest once interviewed a preacher who quit because "the Sabbath came too often." Perhaps the Sabbath will not be such a dreaded day if you build sermon preparation into your routine. There are several steps:
blocks.es_reference: La preparación específica es la preparación que hace en su rutina semanal. Muchos predicadores encuentran la preparación semanal del sermón agotadora. Reader's Digest una vez entrevistó a un predicador que renunció porque "el sábado llegaba con demasiada frecuencia." Quizás el sábado no será un día tan temido si construye la preparación del sermón en su rutina. Hay varios pasos:

blocks.en:
1. Get the idea. Most pastors have difficulty here, and many seem to get the idea from the calendar and the clock. The idea may come from the text, a situation, a need, or a thought that pops into the mind. If you cannot find a text that has the idea you wish to use, it may not be Biblical and should not be preached. Some pastors plan their preaching for a year or so in advance by setting aside a few days for a retreat or study. Keep a sermon pad in your pocket — an idea may come while visiting or while attending a conference. Do not risk losing a good idea.
2. Study the text. Read it and reflect on it. Read the Bible both devotionally and exegetically. Some suggest reading a passage several times before starting to work with it. If you work through books of the Bible by systematic analysis, outlines will emerge naturally from your weekly study pattern.
3. Put down everything. Let your mind be creative. No matter how far-fetched an idea may seem, put it down. Sometimes a large drafting sheet helps for initial brainstorming.
4. Start collecting material. Have the idea at least one week in advance — preferably three months to a year. Some pastors keep 104 folders for upcoming sermon topics; as illustrations and information cross their desks, they drop them in the right folder. When the week arrives, the folder already contains much of the work.
5. Gather other materials. Several Bible translations and paraphrases, linguistic tools (Vine's, Wuest, Barclay for word studies), concordances (Strong's, Young's), commentaries (one or two critical sets such as Word and Interpreter's; devotional authors such as Barclay, McGee, Gutzke, Wiersbe — buy by author, not by set), Bible dictionaries (Interpreter's, Zondervan's Pictorial Encyclopedia), and a thematic index for topical references.

blocks.en: 8.2 The Nine-Step Weekly Rhythm
blocks.es_reference: 8.2 El Ritmo Semanal de Nueve Pasos

blocks.en: Once material is gathered, four further steps take you from raw notes to pulpit:
blocks.es_reference: Una vez reunido el material, cuatro pasos adicionales lo llevan de notas crudas al púlpito:

blocks.en:
6. Arrange the material. Put down a tentative outline. Note references and page numbers for ideas and illustrations you may use within the outline. Later you can type or write the other material into the sermon.
7. Brood over the message. Write down the important ideas. Make any changes in the outline or plan that you need to make. This is a place for imagination and style.
8. Write out the sermon with an oral style. Think of the words as they will sound. Write the body first, then the invitation, and only last the introduction — because the sermon often develops in a different direction than originally anticipated.
9. Prepare to preach. Most immediate preparation can be done on Sunday morning. Read through the sermon slowly; preach it through in your mind before breakfast. (a) Prayer. Spirit-filled sermons are not effortless to produce — they are bathed in fervent prayer. Preaching drives the preacher to his knees with inadequacy more than anything else. (b) Studying and restudying. A sermon is always fresher if it has been working in your soul all week. (c) Go over the sermon on your feet at least twice. Once before the mirror; once in the pastor's study during the first part of Sunday School.

blocks.en: 8.3 Methods of Delivery
blocks.es_reference: 8.3 Métodos de Entrega

blocks.en: John Basigno says that two things are important in preaching: delivery and content. He gives the example of the big league baseball player who earns a huge salary by pitching an inexpensive baseball — the minor leaguer pitches the same ball for a fraction of the salary. The difference is not the baseball but the delivery. A sermon is not a sermon until it has been heard. There are five methods of delivery, and no one method fits everyone — each preacher should discover the way that is most effective for his own gifts.
blocks.es_reference: John Basigno dice que dos cosas son importantes en la predicación: la entrega y el contenido. Da el ejemplo del jugador de béisbol de las grandes ligas que gana un salario enorme lanzando una pelota barata — el ligamenor lanza la misma pelota por una fracción del salario. La diferencia no es la pelota sino la entrega. Un sermón no es un sermón hasta que ha sido escuchado. Hay cinco métodos de entrega, y ningún método único se adapta a todos — cada predicador debe descubrir la manera más efectiva para sus propios dones.

blocks.en:
1. Memorizing. The sermon is written in full and then committed to memory. Very stressful — if one word is forgotten, the preacher may get lost.
2. Reading. The sermon is written beforehand, the notes are carried to the pulpit, and the sermon is read. Jonathan Edwards, Thomas Chalmers, and Peter Marshall all used this method. Not the most popular method, especially in a free-church tradition — many laymen say, "If he is going to read it, he might as well give me the copy and let me read it."
3. Extemporaneous. Preaching without notes or with very limited notes. John Basigno, Norman Vincent Peale, Clarence McCartney, Charles Koller, and V. L. Stanfield all advocate this method. Stanfield calls it "free delivery" — careful preparation, but no notes. Many preachers find it liberating after years of being tied to a manuscript.
4. Limited Notes. Either a brief outline or a highlighted manuscript is carried to the pulpit. Best only for those who can use notes without being tied to them.
5. Impromptu. Speaking at the spur of the moment with limited preparation. Spurgeon sometimes employed something akin to this and succeeded admirably, but it can lead to blunders. Some independent-fundamentalist Baptist preachers once believed it unspiritual to prepare a sermon at all; they tended to be long-winded and repetitious. Do not try to speak impromptu unless you have developed a pronounced talent for this method.

La diferencia no es la pelota sino la entrega. Un sermón no es un sermón hasta que ha sido escuchado. Hay cinco métodos de entrega, y ningún método único se adapta a todos — cada predicador debe descubrir la manera más efectiva para sus propios dones.

blocks.en: 8.4 Five Half-Truths About Delivery
blocks.es_reference: 8.4 Cinco Verdades a Medias Sobre la Entrega

blocks.en: Robert Kirkpatrick warned of five common but incomplete pieces of advice:
blocks.es_reference: Robert Kirkpatrick advirtió sobre cinco piezas de consejo comunes pero incompletas:

blocks.en:
1. "Be natural." The call for naturalness is a reaction against the old preacher's horn — a monotone yelling. The problem is that some people are naturally dull. Preaching is an art and naturally bad habits need correcting. Preaching is to be conversational in manner, but not in emphasis or volume.
2. "Learn to use your body and voice correctly." Too much emphasis on technique can be stifling. The time to focus on techniques is before delivery — during the sermon, allow it to flow unhindered.
3. "Be filled with your subject." You may be so filled with the subject that you forget the object — the audience. Watch for cues: coughing, fidgeting, upright heads, and yawning signal inattention; enthusiastic singing, slightly tilted heads, frequent blinking, smiling and nodding signal engagement.
4. "Desire to help others." The desire to help is no guarantee of effectiveness. Earnest desire cannot overcome defects of style and delivery. Some very sincere preachers are incompetent communicators.
5. "God will provide." God does provide, but rarely when the preacher has not made effort beforehand. As Kirkpatrick said: "It is no more sensible for a preacher to expect a miraculous gift of speech than for a missionary to go to the heathen expecting to receive the gift of tongues."
blocks.es_reference: Robert Kirkpatrick advirtió sobre cinco piezas de consejo comunes pero incompletas:

blocks.en: 8.5 Verbal Aspects of Delivery
blocks.es_reference: 8.5 Aspectos Verbales de la Entrega

blocks.en: Voice projection and volume. Aim the voice slightly upward about ten feet above the congregation. One preacher spoke to a nail on the back wall. Volume should usually begin low — the introduction does not call for a lot of volume. The old black preachers' advice: "Start slow. Stay low. Get higher. Catch fire." At times be loud; at other times speak softly and use a pause of four to five seconds after a profound statement.
blocks.es_reference: Proyección de voz y volumen. Apunte la voz ligeramente hacia arriba unos diez pies sobre la congregación. Un predicador hablaba a un clavo en la pared del fondo. El volumen usualmente debe comenzar bajo — la introducción no requiere mucho volumen. El consejo de los viejos predicadores afroamericanos: "Comience despacio. Manténgase bajo. Suba. Encienda fuego." A veces sea fuerte; otras veces hable suavemente y use una pausa de cuatro a cinco segundos después de una declaración profunda.

blocks.en: Pitch, tone, and inflection. Find your optimum pitch level (about three to five notes above the lowest note you can hit). Three kinds of inflection: downward for a completed thought, upward for question or excitement, circumflex (up and down) for strong doubt or emphasis. Reading fairy tales to children improves inflection — we are naturally expressive with children but inhibited with adults. Beware of raising pitch as volume increases; consciously reach down for a lower note when getting louder.
blocks.es_reference: Proyección de voz y volumen. Apunte la voz ligeramente hacia arriba unos diez pies sobre la congregación. Un predicador hablaba a un clavo en la pared del fondo. El volumen usualmente debe comenzar bajo — la introducción no requiere mucho volumen. El consejo de los viejos predicadores afroamericanos: "Comience despacio. Manténgase bajo. Suba. Encienda fuego." A veces sea fuerte; otras veces hable suavemente y use una pausa de cuatro a cinco segundos después de una declaración profunda.

blocks.en: Rate. Two dangers — speaking too rapidly (nervousness) and speaking too slowly (a greater danger). Faster talkers (around 180 words per minute) are more persuasive than slow or average ones (120-150). A rate twenty to twenty-five percent above average is ideal. The pause can be very effective — Jack Benny would pause before his punch line much longer than other comedians. Use pauses for punctuation, effect, and emphasis. Pause for a moment before beginning to speak; this focuses the audience's attention on you.
blocks.es_reference: Proyección de voz y volumen. Apunte la voz ligeramente hacia arriba unos diez pies sobre la congregación. Un predicador hablaba a un clavo en la pared del fondo. El volumen usualmente debe comenzar bajo — la introducción no requiere mucho volumen. El consejo de los viejos predicadores afroamericanos: "Comience despacio. Manténgase bajo. Suba. Encienda fuego." A veces sea fuerte; otras veces hable suavemente y use una pausa de cuatro a cinco segundos después de una declaración profunda.

blocks.en: Conversational voice and enthusiasm. A good speech is the projection of a good conversation. The monotone yell is the greatest danger to conversational speech. The one characteristic all the great preachers share is enthusiasm — sometimes called zeal, unction, fire, energy. It is not the same as volume, nor as oratory. Most students rate their energy too high; on videotape what felt like a six or seven shows as a two or three. "Preaching from the soul" and "dominating the space" both describe enthusiasm — the preacher's presence occupies all the space he and the audience share.
blocks.es_reference: Proyección de voz y volumen. Apunte la voz ligeramente hacia arriba unos diez pies sobre la congregación. Un predicador hablaba a un clavo en la pared del fondo. El volumen usualmente debe comenzar bajo — la introducción no requiere mucho volumen. El consejo de los viejos predicadores afroamericanos: "Comience despacio. Manténgase bajo. Suba. Encienda fuego." A veces sea fuerte; otras veces hable suavemente y use una pausa de cuatro a cinco segundos después de una declaración profunda.

blocks.en: 8.6 The Body in Delivery
blocks.es_reference: 8.6 El Cuerpo en la Entrega

blocks.en: Albert Mehrabian's research suggests communication is seven percent verbal, thirty-eight percent vocal, and fifty-five percent facial. If words and actions disagree, we tend to believe the actions. Six elements:
blocks.es_reference: La investigación de Albert Mehrabian sugiere que la comunicación es siete por ciento verbal, treinta y ocho por ciento vocal y cincuenta y cinco por ciento facial. Si las palabras y las acciones no concuerdan, tendemos a creer las acciones. Seis elementos:

blocks.en:
1. Authority and confidence. People look for a father figure in a leader. Fear is the great enemy of confidence — fidgeting, rattling change in your pocket, clearing the throat, foot shuffling, stammering, "ah" and "you know" all display lack of poise. Control nervous habits with deep breaths and finger-shaking before the service. Speak with the authority of Scripture — avoid "to my limited knowledge…" or "I don't have all the facts, but…" Billy Graham's "the Bible says…" is very effective.
2. General appearance. The minister's appearance should not call attention to itself. A business suit usually fits, though some preachers targeting younger audiences dress casually. Enter the pulpit with dignity and poise. Take a firm stand a short distance from the pulpit. Do not lean on it or grip its edges — the pulpit is for the Bible and your notes, not to hold you up.
3. Movement. A small pulpit and a lapel mike free movement. Slightly forward is psychologically preferred to a backward defensive hesitation. Some pastors preach the entire sermon in front of the pulpit. Avoid quick jerky movements from nervousness.
4. The face. Smile while preaching; the face needs to appear as though we are delivering the most important message of the hour. Eyebrows raised and lowered; eyes twinkling. Avoid a dead-pan poker face unless delivering a funeral eulogy.
5. Eye contact. Look at the audience constantly. Look at individuals, not at a mass. Maintain contact with some person all the time. Audiences strongly prefer good eye contact.
6. The hands. The hands enhance or detract. Pulling at the ear, twiddling thumbs, stroking a tie or playing with keys disconcerts the audience. When not in use let the hands drop by the side — they will be there when needed. Cultivate gestures: hands, face, and eyes should work together. Above all — sincerity — delivery begins with the personality. Genuine sincerity comes across.

mc.stem: According to Wayne, how many steps are in the weekly sermon preparation workflow he outlines?
mc.why: Nine steps: get the idea, study the text, brainstorm, collect material, gather other materials, arrange/tentative outline, brood and refine, write the sermon, prepare to preach.

mc.stem: Wayne says if you cannot find a text that has the idea you wish to use:
options: It may not be Biblical and should not be preached
You should make up a text
You should preach from your own experience
mc.why: If the idea has no supporting text, the idea is not Biblical and should not be preached.

mc.stem: How far in advance does Wayne recommend having the sermon idea?
options: At least one week, preferably three months to a year
There is no advance preparation needed
mc.why: Best to have the idea at least one week ahead, ideally three months to a year. Some pastors keep 104 folders for the coming year of sermons.

mc.stem: When does Wayne usually write the body of the sermon, the invitation, and the introduction?
options: In that exact order: introduction first, body second, invitation last
Body first, then invitation, then introduction last
He does not write any of them down
mc.why: Wayne writes the body first, then invitation, then introduction. He wants to know what he is introducing before writing the introduction.

mc.stem: John Basigno compares preaching delivery to:
options: A big league baseball player pitching an inexpensive baseball
mc.why: Same ball, vastly different salary — the difference is the delivery, not the content.

mc.stem: Wayne identifies five methods of sermon delivery. Which is NOT one of them?
mc.why: The five methods are: memorizing, reading, extemporaneous (without notes), limited notes, and impromptu. Singing is not a sermon delivery method.

mc.stem: Which method does Wayne believe probably works best for the majority of preachers, even though he does not use it himself?
options: Extemporaneous (with careful preparation but no notes)
mc.why: Wayne notes that extemporaneous preaching (careful preparation, no notes) liberates many preachers, even though it requires some experience and mental capacity.

mc.stem: Wayne lists five 'half-truths about delivery,' adapted from Kirkpatrick. Which is one of them?
options: 'Be natural' — because some people are naturally dull and uninspiring
mc.why: 'Be natural' is a half-truth because some people are naturally dull. Naturally bad habits need to be corrected.

mc.stem: What does Wayne say about the half-truth 'God will provide' regarding sermon delivery?
options: God does provide, but rarely when the preacher has not made effort beforehand in study
God always provides without any effort
God only provides if you fast first
It is not Biblical at all
mc.why: Kirkpatrick (whom Wayne quotes): 'It is no more sensible for a preacher to expect a miraculous gift of speech than for a missionary to go to the heathen expecting to receive the gift of tongues.'

mc.stem: What is the ideal speaking rate for preaching, according to research Wayne cites?
options: About 180 words per minute (20–25% above average)
Whatever feels natural — rate does not matter
mc.why: Faster talkers (180 wpm) were rated more persuasive and favorable than slow or average talkers (120-150 wpm). About 20-25% above average is ideal.

mc.stem: Which comedian did Wayne mention as having mastered the long pause for effect?
mc.why: Jack Benny would pause before delivering his punch line much longer than other comedians, using anticipation.

mc.stem: According to Psychology Today (Albert Mehrabian), what is the percentage breakdown of communication?
mc.why: 7% verbal, 38% vocal, 55% facial. If words and actions conflict, hearers tend to believe the actions.

mc.stem: Buerlein recommends what unusual exercise to relax a singer's facial muscles before performance?
options: Walking into the corner of a room and calling out loudly, 'Blah!'
Reading a Bible verse twenty times
Holding the breath for thirty seconds
mc.why: One famous baritone would walk into a corner and call out 'Blah!' to relax facial muscles. The technique is mentioned as a way to manage pre-preaching tension.

mc.stem: Wayne says that when a preacher's mind goes blank during preaching, the best response is:
options: Read the entire next chapter from the Bible
Repeat what was just said using different words and keep talking until the thought returns
mc.why: Repeat what you just said in different words; eventually the memory returns. Better than awkward pauses or stopping.

mc.stem: What does Wayne say is 'the one characteristic which all the great preachers seem to have in common'?
options: Enthusiasm (sometimes called zeal, unction, fire, energy, power)
mc.why: Enthusiasm. Wayne notes it may be harder for introverts and that all preachers can cultivate it. Volume is not the same as enthusiasm.

mc.stem: The first step in Wayne's nine-step weekly preparation workflow is:
mc.why: Get the idea first — most pastors struggle here; it may come from text, need, or thought.

mc.stem: Which delivery method does Wayne say he used when he was starting out?
mc.why: Wayne memorized at first; its weakness is that forgetting one word can collapse everything.

mc.stem: Wayne's recommended optimum pitch is about how far above your lowest note?
mc.why: About three to five notes above your lowest note; staying on one note is monotone.

mc.stem: The research Wayne cites found that faster talkers (about 180 wpm) were rated as more:
mc.why: Faster talkers were rated more persuasive than slow or average talkers.

mc.stem: According to Mehrabian's research as cited, the largest share of communication is:
mc.why: About 55% is facial/nonverbal — when words and actions conflict, actions win.

sa.prompt: Wayne outlines a nine-step weekly sermon preparation workflow. List all nine steps in order and explain what each step accomplishes.
sa.model: (1) Get the idea — most pastors struggle here. Idea may come from text, situation, need, or thought. Caution: if no text supports it, the idea is not Biblical. (2) Study the text — read it devotionally and exegetically. (3) Brainstorm — put down everything that comes to mind about the text and idea, no matter how far-fetched. (4) Start collecting material — folders for upcoming topics, illustrations on index cards. (5) Gather other materials — translations, linguistic tools, concordances, commentaries. (6) Arrange the material into a tentative outline — references to ideas and illustrations. (7) Brood over the message and refine — imagination and style. (8) Write out the sermon with an oral style — body first, then invitation, then introduction last. (9) Prepare to preach — prayer, restudy, deliver on your feet (Wayne suggests at least twice on Sunday morning). Strong answer notes that the order is intentional and that skipping steps shows up in delivery.

sa.prompt: Compare the five methods of sermon delivery (memorizing, reading, extemporaneous, limited notes, impromptu). Name the preachers Wayne associates with the methods, and note the strengths and weaknesses he gives for each.
sa.model: (1) Memorizing: the sermon is written in full and committed to memory; very stressful, because if one word is forgotten the preacher may get lost. (2) Reading: the sermon is written beforehand and read from the notes carried to the pulpit; Jonathan Edwards, Thomas Chalmers, and Peter Marshall used it; it is not the most popular method, especially in a free-church tradition, where many laymen say, "If he is going to read it, he might as well give me the copy." (3) Extemporaneous: preaching without notes or with very limited notes; John Basigno, Norman Vincent Peale, Clarence McCartney, Charles Koller, and V. L. Stanfield advocate it; Stanfield calls it "free delivery," careful preparation but no notes, and many find it liberating after years tied to a manuscript. (4) Limited notes: a brief outline or highlighted manuscript; best only for those who can use notes without being tied to them. (5) Impromptu: speaking at the spur of the moment with limited preparation; Spurgeon sometimes used something akin to it and succeeded admirably, but it can lead to blunders, and the preachers who thought preparing unspiritual tended to be long-winded and repetitious. No one method fits everyone.

sa.prompt: Take any TWO of Kirkpatrick's five half-truths about delivery (cited by Wayne) and explain why each is dangerous when treated as the whole truth. What balanced advice would replace each half-truth?
sa.model: Strong answers pick any two and explain. Sample for 'Be natural': dangerous because some people are naturally dull, uninspiring, or have bad habits. A savage would beat a seminary student if naturalness were the only criterion. Balanced replacement: be CONVERSATIONAL in manner but not necessarily conversational in emphasis or volume — and consciously correct the bad habits before letting nature take over. Sample for 'Be filled with your subject': dangerous because you may forget the object — the audience. The hearer deserves attention; learn to read cues (inattention shows in fidgeting, coughing, upright unblinking heads; attention shows in singing, slightly tilted heads, frequent blinking). Balanced replacement: be filled with your subject AND watching your audience, ready to adjust. Other half-truths to choose from: 'Learn to use your body and voice correctly' (over-technique stifles), 'Desire to help others' (sincerity alone does not overcome defects), 'God will provide' (only when you have worked).

sa.prompt: Wayne discusses pitch, tone, and inflection in detail. Describe optimum pitch level, the three kinds of inflection, and explain why he recommends reading fairy tales to children as a practice exercise.
sa.model: Optimum pitch level: find the pitch about three to five notes above the lowest note you can hit. The three inflections: (i) downward, for a completed thought; (ii) upward, for a question or excitement; (iii) circumflex (up and down), for strong doubt or emphasis. Why fairy tales to children: reading them improves inflection, because we are naturally expressive with children but inhibited with adults, so the practice trains the voice to be expressive. He also warns to beware of raising pitch as volume increases: consciously reach down for a lower note when getting louder.

sa.prompt: Wayne says the greater danger in speaking rate is NOT speaking too rapidly but speaking too slowly. Defend this counter-intuitive claim using the research he cites, and explain the role of the pause in effective preaching.
sa.model: Wayne names two dangers in the speaking rate: speaking too rapidly (nervousness) and speaking too slowly, which he calls the greater danger. The research he cites: faster talkers (around 180 words per minute) are more persuasive than slow or average ones (120–150 wpm), and a rate twenty to twenty-five percent above average is ideal. The pause is very effective: Jack Benny would pause before his punch line much longer than other comedians. Pauses serve for punctuation, effect, and emphasis; a pause of four to five seconds after a profound statement is powerful, and pausing for a moment before beginning to speak focuses the audience's attention on you. Strong answer notes that a faster rate works together with deliberate pauses.

sa.prompt: Wayne devotes a section to using the body in delivery. Identify at least four of the six elements he covers and explain what is at stake in each.
sa.model: The six elements: (1) Authority and confidence: people look for a leader; fear is the great enemy of confidence, and fidgeting, rattling change, throat-clearing, "ah," and "you know" display lack of poise; speak with the authority of Scripture ("the Bible says…"). (2) General appearance: it should not call attention to itself; enter the pulpit with dignity and poise, and do not lean on it or grip its edges. (3) Movement: slightly forward is psychologically preferred to a backward defensive hesitation; avoid quick jerky movements from nervousness. (4) The face: smile while preaching; Mehrabian's research puts fifty-five percent of communication in the facial; avoid a dead-pan poker face. (5) Eye contact: look at the audience constantly, at individuals and not at a mass; audiences strongly prefer it. (6) The hands: pulling at the ear, twiddling thumbs, or playing with keys disconcerts the audience; when not in use let the hands drop by the side, and cultivate gestures in which hands, face, and eyes work together. Above all is sincerity: delivery begins with the personality, and genuine sincerity comes across.

sa.prompt: Wayne devotes a significant section to enthusiasm in preaching. Define enthusiasm as he distinguishes it from volume and oratory, and explain his concepts of 'preaching from the soul' and 'dominating the space.'
sa.model: Enthusiasm is the one characteristic all the great preachers share, sometimes called zeal, unction, fire, or energy. Wayne distinguishes it from volume and from oratory: it is not the same as either. "Preaching from the soul" and "dominating the space" both describe it: the preacher's presence occupies all the space he and the audience share. Most students rate their own energy too high; on videotape, what felt like a six or seven shows as a two or three.

sa.prompt: A new preacher is so nervous before his first sermon that his hands shake, his throat tightens, and he says 'ah' and 'you know' constantly. Drawing on Wayne's full unit on delivery, prescribe at least five specific actions this preacher should take this week to prepare himself before the next sermon.
sa.model: Strong answers integrate sections of Unit 8 and pick at least five actions tied to the symptoms described. (1) Control nervous habits before the service with deep breaths and finger-shaking, since fidgeting, throat-clearing, "ah," and "you know" display lack of poise. (2) Prepare thoroughly: write out the sermon in an oral style and go over it on his feet at least twice, once before the mirror and once in the pastor's study on Sunday morning. (3) Bathe the sermon in fervent prayer; preaching drives the preacher to his knees with inadequacy. (4) Speak with authority: avoid "to my limited knowledge…" and "I don't have all the facts, but…" and say "the Bible says…" as Billy Graham does. (5) Enter the pulpit with dignity and poise, take a firm stand a short distance from it, and do not lean on it or grip its edges. (6) For the tightened throat, reach for a lower note when getting louder, and read fairy tales aloud to improve inflection. (7) Let the hands drop by the side when not in use.

sa.prompt: List, in order, the nine steps of Wayne's weekly preparation workflow. For any TWO steps, explain why the order matters — what goes wrong if a preacher skips or reverses them.
sa.model: Strong answer lists the nine steps in order (get the idea, study the text, brainstorm, begin gathering material, gather other materials, arrange into a tentative outline, meditate and refine, write the sermon in oral style, prepare to preach) and, for two, explains the cost of skipping/reversing — e.g., writing before gathering produces thin content; skipping meditation produces an unrefined outline.

sa.prompt: A preacher has a naturally soft, monotone voice. Using the unit's teaching on pitch, inflection, rate, and the body, give him four concrete, practical changes he can rehearse this week.
sa.model: Strong answer draws four concrete prescriptions from the unit: vary pitch around the optimum (three to five notes above the lowest), practice the three inflections (downward, upward, circumflex), raise the rate toward ~180 wpm / 20-25% above average, and use the body (eyes, face, controlled movement) to add the nonverbal weight Mehrabian's research highlights. Each should be rehearsable, not abstract.
